lead: A PWM AC chopper switches the load between the 50 Hz supply and a short, at a frequency of a few kilohertz. The fraction of each switching period spent on the supply, the duty ratio D, sets the RMS voltage the load receives. Unlike phase control, no part of the cycle is skipped: the load is fed in every switching period, so the supply current stays close to a sine and the input power factor stays high. A small filter removes the high-frequency ripple.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the phase-control baseline, Unit 1 for IGBT and MOSFET switching and losses, and Unit 4 for the PWM idea.

blocks.text: The power stage has two switches. S1, the series switch, connects the supply to the load. S2, the freewheeling switch, lies across the load. Both must be bidirectional: two IGBTs or MOSFETs joined emitter to emitter, so that one device conducts while the other blocks, in each polarity. A TRIAC is bidirectional but far too slow to switch at kilohertz rates (see Chapter 5.2).

Why bidirectional? The load current is AC. In the positive half cycle it flows one way, in the negative half the other. Each switch must block voltage of either polarity and carry current in both directions, so one device with one antiparallel diode is not enough.

items: S1 closed, S2 open: the load sees the supply voltage v_s.
S1 opens, then S2 closes: the load voltage falls to nearly zero and the load current freewheels through S2.
S2 opens, then S1 closes: the next on-time begins.
The gate signals are complementary with a dead time between them, so S1 and S2 are never on together and the supply is never shorted.

blocks.text: The switching period T is typically 20 µs to 200 µs, that is f_s from 5 kHz to 50 kHz. During the on-time t_on the load is connected; for the rest of T it is shorted. A resistive load sees a rectangular chopped voltage. An inductive load current keeps flowing through S2 during the off-time, smoothed by its own inductance.

sections.h3: Duty ratio, RMS value and harmonics

blocks.text: D = t_on / T,   V_rms = V_s √D,   V_1 = D · V_s
blocks.where: D is the duty ratio, between 0 and 1; t_on is the on-time of the series switch in seconds; T is the switching period in seconds; V_s is the RMS supply voltage in volts; V_rms is the RMS load voltage in volts; V_1 is the RMS value of the supply-frequency component of the load voltage, in volts.

blocks.text: Where V_s√D comes from: the square of the load voltage equals v_s² during t_on and zero otherwise. Its average is D times the average of v_s², so V_rms² = D·V_s² and V_rms = V_s√D.

The chopped waveform is v_s(t) multiplied by a switching function that is 1 for a fraction D of the period and 0 for the rest. Multiplying by a square wave creates sidebands at m·f_s ± f, where m = 1, 2, 3, … and f is the supply frequency. The lowest harmonic sits at f_s − f, which for f_s = 10 kHz and f = 50 Hz is 9950 Hz. The supply-frequency term has value D·v_s, so V_1 = D·V_s.

The input current is the load current gated by the same switching function. For a resistive load the supply-frequency part of the input current is D·v_s/R, exactly in phase with v_s. The gating adds high-frequency ripple, which a small input filter removes. Displacement factor is close to 1, so power factor stays high even at half output; phase control cannot do this, because delaying conduction makes the current lag.

Raising f_s shrinks the filter: inductor and capacitor values fall roughly as 1/f_s, so a 40 kHz chopper needs about one-eighth of the filter a 5 kHz one needs. It also pushes ripple above the audible range. The price is switching loss, which rises roughly in proportion to f_s (see Unit 1). Device loss, gate drive power and heat sink size set the upper limit; 5 kHz to 20 kHz covers most line-frequency designs.

The filter is a small LC low-pass at the input. Its corner frequency sits between 50 Hz and f_s, commonly a few hundred hertz to 2 kHz. It carries the full load current, so the inductor is the bulky part.

items: AC voltage stabilisers and dynamic voltage restorers: a series chopper corrects a feeder voltage sag in milliseconds.
Solid-state tap changers: they replace the mechanical tap changer on a distribution transformer.
Fast lamp dimming, for example in studios and theatres, without the flicker phase control gives at low settings.
Soft starting of induction motors: the voltage rises smoothly as D is increased.

blocks.text: Three-phase versions use three choppers, one per phase, driven from the same duty ratio. Each phase needs its own freewheeling path, and in a three-wire load the freewheeling current must return through the other phases, so the switching patterns are interleaved. Only a few universities teach the three-phase detail. Some syllabi call this whole family an AC chopper or a switched-mode AC controller.

figure.caption: Two switching periods of 100 µs with D = 0.5: the series switch conducts for 50 µs, then the freewheeling switch takes over, so the load voltage alternates between the supply voltage and zero.

spec.aria: Two switching periods of 100 microseconds show the series switch on for the first 50 microseconds and the freewheel switch on for the next 50, with the load voltage alternating between supply voltage and zero.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 50 Ω resistive load through a single-phase PWM AC chopper with a freewheeling switch. The switching frequency is 10 kHz and the duty ratio is D = 0.6. Find the on-time, the RMS load voltage, the load power, the RMS value of the supply-frequency component of the load voltage, and the frequency of the lowest harmonic in the load voltage.
steps: Switching period T = 1/f_s = 1/10 000 Hz = 100 µs. On-time t_on = D·T = 0.6 × 100 µs = 60 µs.
RMS load voltage: V_rms = V_s√D = 230 × √0.6 = 230 × 0.7746 = 178.2 V.
Supply-frequency component: V_1 = D·V_s = 0.6 × 230 = 138.0 V. It is smaller than V_rms, as it must be.
The lowest harmonic lies at f_s − f = 10 000 − 50 = 9950 Hz, harmonic order 199. The next ones sit at f_s + f = 10 050 Hz and around 2f_s.
examples.answer: t_on = 60 µs, V_rms = 178.2 V, P = 634.8 W, supply-frequency component 138.0 V, lowest harmonic at 9950 Hz, about 200 times the supply frequency.
examples.check:
import math
Vs = 230.0
D = 0.6
R = 50.0
fs = 10000.0
f = 50.0
T = 1.0/fs
ton = D*T
Vrms = Vs*math.sqrt(D)
P = Vrms**2/R
V1 = D*Vs
flow = fs - f
print(round(ton*1e6, 1))
print(round(Vrms, 1))
print(round(P, 1))
print(round(V1, 1))
print(round(flow))

traps: V_o = D·V_s is the supply-frequency component, not the RMS value. The RMS value of the chopped waveform is V_s√D, which is always larger: 178.2 V against 138.0 V at D = 0.6.
With no dead time, S1 and S2 conduct together and the supply is shorted through two devices. The current spike destroys them.
One IGBT with an antiparallel diode is not a bidirectional switch; it blocks only one polarity. Two devices back to back are needed.
The freewheeling switch carries the full load current when the series switch is off. Ignoring 1–2 V of device drop is fine at 230 V, but not at 12 V.
The input filter corner must sit well below f_s. A corner too near the switching frequency leaves ripple on the supply current and spoils the power factor.

quiz.q: State the RMS load voltage of an ideal PWM AC chopper feeding a resistive load.
quiz.a: V_rms = V_s√D, where V_s is the RMS supply voltage in volts and D is the duty ratio.

quiz.q: Why must both switches in the chopper be bidirectional?
quiz.a: The load current reverses every supply half cycle. Each switch must block voltage of either polarity and conduct current in both directions, so two devices are connected back to back.

quiz.q: Why is a dead time needed between the gate signals of S1 and S2?
quiz.a: If both conduct at once the supply is shorted through S1 and S2, and the current is limited only by device and wiring resistance. Dead time keeps both off briefly at each transition.

quiz.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 20 Ω resistor through a PWM AC chopper with D = 0.4. Find the RMS load voltage and the load power.
Explain why the input power factor of a PWM AC chopper stays high at reduced output while a phase controller's falls.
quiz.a: The chopper connects the load to the supply in every switching period with the same pattern, so the supply-frequency part of the input current stays in phase with the supply voltage and the displacement angle is near zero. Phase control delays the start of conduction by α, so the current lags and the displacement factor falls to about cos α.

quiz.q: What happens when the switching frequency is raised from 5 kHz to 40 kHz?
quiz.a: Filter size falls about eight times and ripple moves above hearing, but switching loss and gate drive power rise roughly eight times, so efficiency drops and the heat sink grows.

quiz.q: At what frequency does the lowest load-voltage harmonic appear when f_s = 20 kHz and the supply is 50 Hz?

beyond: Not for the exam. SiC and GaN devices push AC choppers to tens of kilohertz while keeping filters small, which is what makes compact solid-state transformers and dynamic voltage restorers practical. Repeat the same two-switch cell nine times and you arrive at the matrix converter of Chapter 5.6. Power-quality standards now reward fast voltage correction at the point of common coupling, where the chopper competes with the series converter of a unified power flow controller. Search for 'AC chopper', 'PWM AC voltage regulator' and 'dynamic voltage restorer' to go further.
